Project Name

ASTRAS — Earth Analogs for Moon and Mars Exploration

Summary

ASTRAS is an interactive platform for identifying and investigating Earth landscapes that resemble locations on the Moon and Mars. It combines three-dimensional planetary exploration, measured terrain comparisons, research-guided missions, and downloadable scientific reports.

Users can explore 20 planetary destinations and eight terrestrial regions, including Ustyurt, Atacama, Rio Tinto, Hawaii, and Antarctica. The application compares Earth elevation data with prepared NASA LOLA and HiRISE terrain targets using consistent spatial scales, slope distributions, and elevation relief.

ASTRAS makes planetary analog research more accessible and transparent: users can inspect paired surfaces, examine elevation profiles, consult scientific publications, and export evidence. It supports exploration and candidate screening while clearly distinguishing terrain similarity from geological equivalence or mission safety.
details:
ASTRAS connects planetary exploration with evidence-based investigation of terrestrial analogs. Our goal is to help students, educators, and researchers understand why an Earth landscape may be useful for studying a specific lunar or Martian environment.

The application integrates Earth, Moon, and Mars into one interactive workspace. Users can explore planetary destinations, select a terrestrial research region, inspect candidate terrain windows, and compare Earth and planetary surfaces using synchronized 3D views, elevation colours, contours, and profiles.

Our Earth catalog covers eight regions and contains 2,261 usable terrain windows across surveyed areas totaling 828 square kilometres. Quantitative comparisons currently use two prepared planetary targets: the Shackleton region on the Moon, derived from NASA LOLA data, and Jezero crater on Mars, derived from HiRISE data. Earth elevations come from Copernicus GLO-30.

Comparisons use 600 × 600 metre windows aggregated into 10 × 10 grids. An exploratory distance combines slope-distribution differences and normalized elevation-relief differences. Candidates are ranked within the selected region, rather than presented as globally optimal locations.

Four-stop guided missions connect exploration with questions based on published research. Users can download scientific PDF reports containing coordinates, visualizations, metrics, references, and data hashes, alongside machine-readable evidence.

We developed the project using TypeScript, React, Three.js, Vite, Python, and jsPDF. Remotion was used to create the demonstration video.

Our creative contribution is the connection between an exploratory planetary interface and inspectable scientific evidence. We explicitly communicate limitations: terrain similarity does not establish matching geology, habitability, landing safety, or suitability for a permanent base. Published biological and geochemical findings provide context; their raw laboratory measurements were not imported.
